speechtext:
I rise this evening, Mr. Speaker, to pursue a question I asked on March 19 regarding certain n.s.f. cheques written for services in my area by the now bankrupt subcontractor on the Bath-Millhav-en federal prison complex, D. Leblanc Inc. of Chomedey, Laval, Quebec. I brought up this matter on February 25 when I interceded on behalf of those who had received n.s.f. cheques for labour on this project.
I am not here tonight to embarass the government. The government is certainly embarrassed enough already, due to the fact that this subcontractor was not bonded. I thank the minister for his response to my plea of February 25 when he assured me and the labouring men of my riding who have been so rudely treated that $30,000 would be withheld from progress payments to Argo, the prime contractor, and applied toward payment of n.s.f. cheques submitted to Argo for labour.
However, there is another side to this serious question and it is this1 aspect which I am raising tonight. Leblanc, in its capacity as a contractor on this job, arranged for several of its key personnel to obtain lodging, room and board in the vicinity of the prison site. In one case, these services were provided by the Millhaven Inn, a small hostel operated by L. G. Savage of Bath, Ontario. Leblanc agreed to pay for lodging for his men at this establishment, and I have here photostat copies of these n.s.f. cheques given to Mr. Savage for his services. I also have a photostat copy of the total owing to Mr. Savage by Leblanc, namely, $1,099.50.
These cheques were, of course, for services, not directly for labour. Mr. Savage told me in a letter of March 10 that he had contacted the Argo claims representative, a Mr. Caron in Montreal who was handling the Argo-Leblanc affairs and Mr. Caron stated that as far as Argo was concerned Mr. Savage and any other local people holding Leblanc n.s.f. cheques for services had no hope of getting their money because they-meaning Argo, the
April 1, 1969

surviving prime contractor-were interested only ini labour, that is, wages.
It is a fine situation, Mr. Speaker, when an unbonded contractor, an unknown in our province, can get a contract from the federal government, come in from Quebec, or any other province, obtain thousands of dollars worth of labour and services, pay for them, supposedly, with worthless cheques and then disappear into his native province while his debts and obligations go unsatisfied. This cannot be allowed, Mr. Speaker. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) were here tonight I would say to him that this is a long way from the just society he advocates. In fact, I would make a wager with the Prime Minister or any of his members that no contractor from Ontario would be able to get a federal job in Quebec. There would be some technical point or option whereby this government and the provincial authorities in Quebec would make sure a federal government contract in the province of Quebec would be awarded to a Quebec contractor. I am not saying that is not a good idea, for Quebec, Mr. Speaker. For example, just last week when awarding defence contracts for the new green uniforms for the unified forces Quebec received the lion's share of these contracts.
I now cite the case of Napanee Industries who last year lost a $3 million equipment contract for the C.N.R. The successful bidders were Quebec firms which were provincially subsidized for their success in getting federal contracts. This, of course, was not a building contract. It was a manufacturing contract for flatcars and railway equipment. This type of business hurt us badly in Napanee because it forced Napanee Industries to lay off many men at the beginning of the winter. It is time that Canadians, region to region and province to province stopped this deception, intrigue and discrimination and became forthright and honest with each other.
The government three weeks ago assumed basic responsibility for all n.s.f. cheques issued by D. Leblanc Inc. at the Bath Millhaven project to the extent of $30,000. They must also assume this responsibility to Mr. Savage for the n.s.f. cheques that Mr. Savage has accepted for services.
I have a copy of Mr. Savage's letter from which I quote:
As arranged with D. Leblanc, C. Leblanc and C. Pomerleau, owners of the company, all accounts to the Millhaven Inn would be paid by the company and they in turn would deduct, room, board and rent from the employees, thus avoiding any loss to us in the event of layoffs or strikes.
